result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.add_johnson_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add a Johnson graph J(n, k) to this graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L7731-L7877){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.add_johnson_graph( n, k, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Johnson graph](/assets/graphs/add-johnson-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three Johnson graphs side by side, each node labeled with its subset. J(3, 1) is a triangle on 0, 1, 2 and J(4, 1) is a complete graph on four singletons; J(4, 2) is a hexagon of the six pairs from 0 to 3, where two pairs are joined when they share one element, so only complementary pairs such as 0,1 and 2,3 stay unjoined." width="100%"} Creates a graph where nodes represent `k`-subsets of `{0, 1, ..., n-1}`, and two nodes are adjacent if their subsets intersect in exactly `k-1` elements (i.e., they differ by exactly one element). Moving along an edge means swapping one element of the subset for one outside it, so the shortest-path distance between two nodes counts how many swaps separate their subsets. Johnson graphs are distance-regular and `k(n-k)`-regular. They generalize to the family `J(n,k,s)` where `s` is the intersection size; this method implements the standard case where `s = k - 1`. When `k = 0` or `k = n`, the graph is trivial (single node, no edges). Each node is labelled with the elements of its subset, comma-separated and in increasing order (e.g. `"0,2"`; the empty subset from `k=0` gets the label `""`). Nodes are created in lexicographic order of their subsets and appended to the graph, with IDs continuing from the existing nodes; existing nodes are left untouched and never connected to the new ones. In a directed graph each edge points from the earlier subset to the later one in that order. Johnson graphs come up in: - combinatorics and coding theory (constant-weight codes, association schemes) - modeling state spaces where a configuration is a fixed-size selection and a move swaps one item in for another (e.g. team rosters or portfolios of fixed size) - testing algorithms on highly symmetric, regular graphs with known properties ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Size of the base set `{0, 1, ..., n-1}`. Must be non-negative. [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Size of each subset. Must satisfy `0 <= k <= n`. Because `J(n, k)` and `J(n, n-k)` have the same structure, `k` and `n - k` give equivalent graphs (with different labels). `k=1` gives a complete graph on `n` nodes. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `k=` > `n=`, or if one of the subset labels is already used in the graph (e.g. by an earlier Johnson graph); nothing is added in that case. [OverflowError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` or `k=` is negative. ::: ## Properties {.doc-properties} - **Nodes**: `C(n,k)` nodes, where `C` is the binomial coefficient "n choose k" - **Edges**: `C(n,k) * k(n-k) / 2` - **Degree**: each node has degree `k(n-k)` (regular graph) - **Diameter**: `min(k, n-k)` - **Distance-regular**: for any two nodes at distance `d`, how many neighbors of one lie at distance `d - 1`, `d`, or `d + 1` from the other depends only on `d` - **No self-loops or multi-edges** ## Relationship To Other Graphs {.doc-relationship-to-other-graphs} - **Complete graphs**: `J(n,1)` is the complete graph on `n` nodes. - **Kneser graphs K(n,k)**: nodes are adjacent if their subsets are disjoint. For `k=2`, `J(n,2)` and `K(n,2)` are complements of each other. - **Petersen graph**: `K(5,2)`, the complement of `J(5,2)`, is the Petersen graph (10 nodes, degree 3). `J(5,2)` itself has degree 6. ## Complexity {.doc-complexity} - Time: `O(C(n,k)^2 * k)`, since every pair of subsets is compared - Space: `O(C(n,k) + edges)` `C(n,k)` grows very quickly (e.g. `C(20,10)` is 184,756), so keep `n=` modest when `k=` is near `n / 2`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} `J(4,2)` has one node per 2-element subset of `{0,1,2,3}`, and `C(4,2) = 6` such subsets exist: ::: {#14efd4f4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_johnson_graph(n=4, k=2) graph.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 6 ``` ::: ::: Each pair of subsets that differ by exactly one element gets an edge, giving `12` edges here: ::: {#1536fcdd .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 12 ``` ::: ::: Node labels spell out the subsets themselves, so you can read off which elements each node represents: ::: {#eebe0e7f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} nodes = [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in sorted(graph.get_node_ids(limit=None))] nodes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['0,1', '0,2', '0,3', '1,2', '1,3', '2,3'] ``` ::: ::: Since nodes are labelled by their subsets, you can look them up directly. The neighbors of `"0,1"` are the four pairs that share exactly one element with it; only its complement `"2,3"` is missing: ::: {#ecab5678 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} sorted(graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.neighbors("0,1")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['0,2', '0,3', '1,2', '1,3'] ``` ::: ::: Every node touches the same number of neighbors, since Johnson graphs are regular with degree `k(n-k)`. For `k=2, n=4` that's `2*2 = 4`, so every node should report the same degree: ::: {#dbc99b27 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} degrees = [graph.get_degree(nid) for nid in graph.get_node_ids(limit=None)] set(degrees) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` {4} ``` ::: ::: `J(5,2)` has `C(5,2) = 10` nodes, and its degree formula gives `2*(5-2) = 6`, for `10*6/2 = 30` edges: ::: {#50b091ef .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} johnson_5_2 = ec.Graph(directed=False).add_johnson_graph(n=5, k=2) johnson_5_2.count_nodes(), johnson_5_2.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (10, 30) ``` ::: ::: Note that despite looking similar on paper, `J(5,2)` is not the Petersen graph -- that's actually the Kneser graph `K(5,2)`, which is the complement of `J(5,2)`. `J(5,2)` has 10 nodes and is 6-regular, while the Petersen graph has 10 nodes but is only 3-regular: ::: {#f1ff4e9b .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} {johnson_5_2.get_degree(nid) for nid in johnson_5_2.get_node_ids(limit=None)} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` {6} ``` ::: :::
